title: Development and validation of the Visual Stress Scale (VSS) in a parent sample
abstract: Abstract Single-item measures offer a low-burden alternative to the lengthy questionnaires typically used to assess parental stress. For single-item measures, graphical formats using pictorial or metaphor-based illustrations have been recommended; however, no such graphic single-item instrument currently exists for assessing stress. We therefore developed the Visual Stress Scale (VSS). Convergent, and concurrent validity, as well as test–retest reliability of the VSS, were examined in a sample of 329 parents in Germany using two online surveys with a two-week retest interval. The VSS correlated positively with established stress measures (Parenting Stress Index: r = .44–.55; Perceived Stress Questionnaire1. By convention, correlation coefficients and other measures that take values between 0 and 1 are reported without a leading zero before the decimal point. A few extra spaces have inadvertently been introduced, but unfortunately, I am unable to remove them.: r = .66, DASS-21 Stress subscale: r = .68) and showed a strong loading alongside the PSQ items in the one-factor model (λ = .62, all p s < .001). Higher VSS scores were associated with higher depression ( r = .67) and anxiety ( r = .43), and with lower well-being ( r = –.63) and perceived social support ( r = –.37; all p s < .001). Test–retest reliability was moderate among participants successfully matched across the two measurement time points ( ICC (2,1) = .56, p < .001). The exploratory factor analysis provided preliminary insights into how the VSS relates to different aspects of parental stress within Abidin’s framework [1]. Overall, the findings provide initial evidence for the convergence of the VSS with established stress measures, its two-week temporal stability, and its expected associations with theoretically related constructs. The VSS may be particularly useful in high-burden settings. Further research is needed to examine its discriminant validity, particularly whether it assesses stress specifically or reflects broader psychological distress, and to evaluate its psychometric properties using different study designs and populations.
